name: Cholic acid
text:
Cholic acid is one of the two main bile acids that the liver makes from cholesterol. It is a white crystalline substance that does not dissolve in water; its salts are called cholates.

As a food additive it is classed as an emulsifier, a substance that helps fat and water mix.

name: Choline salts and esters
text:
This group covers compounds of choline: choline acetate, carbonate, chloride, citrate, tartrate and lactate. Choline is an essential nutrient found in foods such as liver, egg yolks and dairy products.

As food additives these compounds are classed as emulsifiers, which help keep fat and water mixed. Choline chloride and choline bitartrate are also used in dietary supplements.

name: Amylases
text:
Amylases are enzymes that break starch down into sugars. They occur naturally in human saliva and the pancreas, as well as in plants, fungi and bacteria. For food use amylase may be obtained from pig pancreas or from moulds, and some amylases are produced by bacteria such as Bacillus species.

As a food additive amylase is classed as a flour treatment agent. In breadmaking it turns starch in flour into sugars that yeast can ferment, and amylases are also important in brewing.

Bakers with long exposure to amylase-enriched flour are at risk of developing dermatitis or asthma.

name: Proteases
text:
Proteases are enzymes that break down proteins. The group includes papain from papaya, bromelain from pineapple, ficin from the latex of fig trees, and proteases produced by microorganisms such as Aspergillus oryzae and Bacillus subtilis.

As food additives they are classed as flour treatment agents, flavour enhancers and stabilisers. Papain and bromelain are widely used to tenderise meat, proteases are added to bread improvers, and ficin has been used in making freeze-resistant beer.

name: Glucose oxidase
text:
Glucose oxidase is an enzyme that uses oxygen to oxidise glucose, producing gluconic acid and hydrogen peroxide. It is made by certain fungi, such as Aspergillus niger, and by some insects; honeybees add it to honey, where it acts as a natural preservative.

As a food additive it is classed as an antioxidant. It is used to remove oxygen and glucose from packaged foods such as dried egg powder, preventing unwanted browning and off-flavours, and it strengthens dough in baking.

name: Invertase
text:
Invertase is an enzyme that splits sucrose into glucose and fructose, producing invert sugar syrup. It is made by many organisms, including bees, which use it to make honey; for industrial use it is usually obtained from yeast.

As a food additive it is classed as a stabiliser. In chocolate-covered sweets, cordials and fondants it liquefies the sugar, giving soft or liquid centres.

name: Lipases
text:
Lipases are enzymes that break down fats, releasing fatty acids. They are generally obtained from animal sources, but can also be produced by microorganisms.

As a food additive lipase is classed as a flavour enhancer. Lipase from the pregastric (mouth and throat) tissues of calves, young goats and lambs has been used in cheese making for centuries: the fatty acids it releases from milk fat enhance the flavour of the cheese.

name: Lysozyme
text:
Lysozyme is an enzyme that breaks down the cell walls of bacteria, especially Gram-positive bacteria. It occurs in tears, saliva, human milk and mucus, and in large amounts in egg white; the food additive is obtained from hen egg white.

It is used as a preservative in cheese making, beer and wine. In ripened cheeses it helps prevent the late gas formation ("blowing") caused by Clostridium bacteria.

Because it comes from egg, residues in treated foods may trigger allergic reactions in people sensitive to egg.

name: Polydextrose
text:
Polydextrose is a synthetic polymer of glucose. It is made by heating glucose with about 10 percent sorbitol and a small amount of citric or phosphoric acid. It counts as soluble fibre and provides about 1 kcal per gram.

It is used as a bulking agent, humectant, stabiliser and thickener, and replaces sugar, starch or fat in drinks, cakes, sweets, desserts, breakfast cereals and salad dressings.

Large amounts can have a laxative effect and cause intestinal gas.

name: Polyvinylpyrrolidone
text:
Polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP), also called povidone, is a synthetic water-soluble polymer made from N-vinylpyrrolidone. When taken by mouth, little or none of it is absorbed into the body.

As a food additive it is classed as a stabiliser, thickener, dispersing agent and coating agent. In food its use is mainly in food supplements such as tablets; in medicines it is a common tablet binder.

name: Polyvinylpolypyrrolidone
text:
Polyvinylpolypyrrolidone (PVPP), also called crospovidone, is a highly cross-linked form of polyvinylpyrrolidone. It does not dissolve in water but absorbs it and swells rapidly, which makes it useful as a disintegrant in tablets, including food supplements.

In winemaking and brewing it is used as a processing aid that binds polyphenols and tannins, giving clear beers with stable foam. It is then removed by filtration, so only negligible amounts remain in the drink.

name: Polyvinyl alcohol
text:
Polyvinyl alcohol is a synthetic water-soluble polymer. It is not made from its own monomer but by hydrolysis of polyvinyl acetate.

As a food additive it is classed as a coating and sealing agent and as a binder. Its food use is mainly as a coating for food supplements in tablet form.

name: Pullulan
text:
Pullulan is a polysaccharide made of glucose units. It is produced by fermenting hydrolysed starch with the fungus Aureobasidium pullulans.

It is edible and almost tasteless, and its main commercial use is in edible films such as breath-freshening strips. It is also used to make capsules, as a vegetarian alternative to gelatine, and as a glazing agent and thickener.

Part of it is not digested and is fermented in the gut; large amounts can cause flatulence.

name: Basic methacrylate copolymer
text:
Basic methacrylate copolymer is a synthetic polymer made from three monomers: methyl methacrylate, butyl methacrylate and dimethylaminoethyl methacrylate. The solid polymer does not dissolve in water, but films made from it dissolve in stomach acid.

It is used as a glazing and coating agent on solid food supplements such as tablets, where the coating protects against moisture and masks taste or odour. Because of its large molecular size it is not absorbed by the body.

name: Neutral methacrylate copolymer
text:
Neutral methacrylate copolymer is a synthetic polymer made from methyl methacrylate and ethyl acrylate by emulsion polymerisation. It is supplied as a dispersion in water.

It is used as a glazing agent to coat food supplements in solid form, such as tablets and capsules, but not chewable ones. It is essentially not absorbed by the body.

name: Anionic methacrylate copolymer
text:
Anionic methacrylate copolymer is a synthetic polymer made from methacrylic acid, methyl methacrylate and methyl acrylate by emulsion polymerisation. It is supplied as a dispersion in water.

It is used as a coating agent for food supplements in solid form, such as tablets and capsules, but not chewable ones. It is essentially not absorbed by the body.

name: Polyvinylpyrrolidone-vinyl acetate copolymer
text:
Polyvinylpyrrolidone-vinyl acetate copolymer, also called copovidone, is a synthetic polymer made by copolymerising N-vinyl-2-pyrrolidone with vinyl acetate.

It is used as a binding and coating agent in food supplements in solid form, such as tablets, but not chewable ones. Little of it is absorbed when swallowed; most passes through the gut unchanged and is excreted.

name: Polyvinyl alcohol-polyethylene glycol graft copolymer
text:
This is a synthetic graft copolymer made of about 75 percent polyvinyl alcohol units and 25 percent polyethylene glycol units. It is a white to faintly yellow powder.

It is used to make quick-dissolving film coatings for food supplements in solid form, such as tablets and capsules, but not chewable ones. Its absorption by the body is negligible.

name: Carbomer
text:
Carbomer is a synthetic polymer of acrylic acid whose chains are cross-linked with allyl pentaerythritol.

The EU added it to its list of food additives in 2023 for use in food supplements only. In solid supplements it acts as a bulking agent and stabiliser, giving a controlled, extended release of nutrients and allowing smaller tablets that are easier to swallow; in liquid supplements it is a stabiliser and thickener.

In 2021 EFSA found no evidence that carbomer is absorbed or transformed in the body and no concern about genotoxicity, and set an acceptable daily intake of 190 mg/kg body weight per day.

name: Dextrins
text:
Dextrins are carbohydrates made of glucose units, with shorter chains than starch. For industrial use they are made by roasting dry starch, with or without a little acid. They are white, yellow or brown powders that dissolve partly or fully in water, giving solutions of low viscosity.

As a food additive dextrin is classed as a thickener, stabiliser, emulsifier and carrier. White dextrins are used to add crispness to batters, coatings and glazes.

name: Acid-treated starch
text:
Acid-treated starch, also called thin-boiling starch, is made by treating starch with an inorganic acid such as hydrochloric acid. This partly breaks down the starch molecules and lowers the viscosity of the cooked starch.

As a food additive it is classed as a thickener, stabiliser and emulsifier. One example of its use is forming the shell of jelly beans.

name: Alkaline-treated starch
text:
Alkaline-treated starch is a modified starch made by treating starch with an alkali such as sodium hydroxide or potassium hydroxide.

As a food additive it is classed as a thickener, stabiliser and emulsifier, like other modified starches.

name: Bleached starch
text:
Bleached starch is a modified starch that has been whitened by treatment with a bleaching agent such as hydrogen peroxide.

As a food additive it is classed as a thickener, stabiliser and emulsifier, like other modified starches.

name: Oxidised starch
text:
Oxidised starch is made by treating starch in an alkaline slurry with sodium hypochlorite. Because of this it is sometimes called "chlorinated" starch, although its structure contains no chlorine. The treatment lowers the viscosity of the cooked starch.

As a food additive it is classed as a thickener, stabiliser and emulsifier. It is used, for example, to make batter stickier.

name: Enzyme-treated starch
text:
Enzyme-treated starch is starch that has been partly broken down by enzymes such as amylases, giving shorter carbohydrate chains. Products made this way include maltodextrin and cyclodextrin.

As a food additive it is classed as a thickener, stabiliser and emulsifier.

name: Monostarch phosphate
text:
Monostarch phosphate is a modified starch made by esterifying starch with orthophosphoric acid, sodium or potassium orthophosphate, or sodium tripolyphosphate. The phosphate groups reduce retrogradation, the gradual stiffening and water loss of cooked starch, and let the starch absorb more water.

As a food additive it is classed as a thickener, stabiliser and emulsifier.

It is not absorbed intact: intestinal enzymes break much of it down, and the rest is fermented by gut bacteria.

name: Distarch glycerol
text:
Distarch glycerol is a chemically modified starch. It is made by treating starch with a small amount of epichlorohydrin under alkaline conditions, which links neighbouring starch chains through glycerol bridges, roughly one link per 220 glucose units.

Like other modified starches, it was intended for use as a thickener in food.

name: Distarch phosphate
text:
Distarch phosphate is a modified starch made by treating starch with sodium trimetaphosphate or phosphorus oxychloride. These reagents cross-link the starch chains with phosphate bridges, which changes the texture and flow properties of the thickened food.

As a food additive it is classed as a thickener, stabiliser and emulsifier.

It is not absorbed intact: intestinal enzymes break much of it down, and the rest is fermented by gut bacteria.

name: Phosphated distarch phosphate
text:
Phosphated distarch phosphate is a modified starch that combines the treatments used for monostarch phosphate (E1410) and distarch phosphate (E1412): the starch chains are cross-linked by phosphate bridges and also esterified with phosphate. The starting starch can come from wheat, potato, tapioca or other plants.

It is used as a thickener, stabiliser and emulsifier. Because it stays stable through freezing and thawing, it is used in products such as soups, sauces, frozen gravies and pie fillings.

In 2017 EFSA concluded that modified starches raise no safety concern at the reported uses and that no numerical acceptable daily intake is needed.

name: Acetylated distarch phosphate
text:
Acetylated distarch phosphate is a modified starch that is cross-linked with sodium trimetaphosphate or phosphorus oxychloride and esterified with acetic anhydride or vinyl acetate.

It is used as a thickener, stabiliser and emulsifier. It is not absorbed intact: it is largely broken down by intestinal enzymes and then fermented by gut bacteria.

In 2017 EFSA concluded that modified starches raise no safety concern at the reported uses and that no numerical acceptable daily intake is needed.

name: Acetylated starch
text:
Acetylated starch, also called starch acetate, is a modified starch esterified with acetic anhydride or vinyl acetate.

It is used as a thickener and stabiliser, and is also listed as an emulsifier. It is not absorbed intact: it is largely broken down by intestinal enzymes and then fermented by gut bacteria.

In 2017 EFSA concluded that modified starches raise no safety concern at the reported uses and that no numerical acceptable daily intake is needed.

name: Starch acetate esterified with vinyl acetate
text:
This is a modified starch: starch converted into starch acetate using vinyl acetate as the acetylating reagent. Its functions are those of a thickener, stabiliser, emulsifier and bulking agent.

Starch acetylated with vinyl acetate is now covered by the specification for acetylated starch (E1420), which allows either acetic anhydride or vinyl acetate as the reagent.

name: Acetylated distarch adipate
text:
Acetylated distarch adipate is a modified starch cross-linked with adipic anhydride and esterified with acetic anhydride. The treatment makes the starch more resistant to high temperatures.

It is used as a thickener and stabiliser, and is also listed as an emulsifier.

In 2017 EFSA concluded that modified starches raise no safety concern at the reported uses and that no numerical acceptable daily intake is needed.

name: Acetylated distarch glycerol
text:
Acetylated distarch glycerol is a modified starch whose chains are cross-linked by glycerol bridges, formed by treating the starch with epichlorohydrin, and which is also acetylated. Its functions are those of a thickener and emulsifier.

In 1982 the Joint FAO/WHO Expert Committee on Food Additives (JECFA) allocated it no acceptable daily intake and withdrew its specification.

name: Distarch glycerol
text:
Distarch glycerol (also written distarch glycerine) is a modified starch whose chains are cross-linked by glycerol diether bridges. These form when starch is treated with epichlorohydrin under alkaline conditions.

It belongs to the cross-linked modified starches, which are used as thickeners and stabilisers. In international and Russian additive lists the same substance carries the number 1411 (E1411).

name: Hydroxypropyl starch
text:
Hydroxypropyl starch is a modified starch etherified with propylene oxide. The treatment improves the stability of the starch's thickening power.

It is used as a thickener, stabiliser and emulsifier.

In 2017 EFSA concluded that modified starches raise no safety concern at the reported uses and that no numerical acceptable daily intake is needed.

name: Hydroxypropyl distarch glycerol
text:
Hydroxypropyl distarch glycerol (also written hydroxypropyl distarch glycerine) is a modified starch made with two reagents: a small amount of epichlorohydrin, which cross-links the starch chains, and propylene oxide, which adds hydroxypropyl groups. Its functions are those of a thickener and emulsifier. In Russian additive rules the same substance has carried the number E1443.

In 1982 the Joint FAO/WHO Expert Committee on Food Additives (JECFA) allocated it no acceptable daily intake and withdrew its specification.

name: Hydroxypropyl distarch phosphate
text:
Hydroxypropyl distarch phosphate is a modified starch cross-linked with sodium trimetaphosphate or phosphorus oxychloride and etherified with propylene oxide.

It is used as a thickener, stabiliser and emulsifier, and also as an anti-caking agent.

In 2017 EFSA concluded that modified starches raise no safety concern at the reported uses and that no numerical acceptable daily intake is needed.

name: Hydroxypropyl distarch glycerol
text:
Hydroxypropyl distarch glycerol is a modified starch made with two reagents: a small amount of epichlorohydrin, which cross-links the starch chains, and propylene oxide, which adds hydroxypropyl groups. Its functions are those of a thickener and emulsifier. The same substance also appears under the number E1441.

In 1982 the Joint FAO/WHO Expert Committee on Food Additives (JECFA) allocated it no acceptable daily intake and withdrew its specification.

name: Starch sodium octenyl succinate
text:
Starch sodium octenyl succinate is a modified starch esterified with octenylsuccinic anhydride. The octenyl groups make the starch partly fat-attracting, which is why it works as an emulsifier.

It is used as an emulsifier, stabiliser and thickener, including in infant formulae and baby foods, and as a carrier for added nutrients such as vitamins. It is not absorbed intact: it is largely broken down by intestinal enzymes and then fermented by gut bacteria.

In 2017 EFSA concluded that modified starches raise no safety concern at the reported uses and that no numerical acceptable daily intake is needed.

name: Acetylated oxidised starch
text:
Acetylated oxidised starch is a modified starch that is first treated with sodium hypochlorite (oxidised) and then esterified with acetic anhydride.

It is used as a thickener, stabiliser and emulsifier.

In 2017 EFSA concluded that modified starches raise no safety concern at the reported uses and that no numerical acceptable daily intake is needed.

name: Starch aluminium octenyl succinate
text:
Starch aluminium octenyl succinate is a modified starch esterified with octenylsuccinic anhydride and then treated with aluminium sulphate.

Its functions are those of an anti-caking agent, carrier and stabiliser. It is used to encapsulate vitamin preparations in food supplements.

In 2017 EFSA concluded that modified starches, this one included, raise no safety concern at the reported uses and that no numerical acceptable daily intake is needed.

name: Benzylated hydrocarbons
text: Benzylated hydrocarbons are synthetic hydrocarbons that carry benzyl groups; the name covers a group of compounds rather than one defined substance. The number sits in the series used for carriers and solvents, but no specific food use of this substance is documented.

name: Butane-1,3-diol
text:
Butane-1,3-diol, also called 1,3-butylene glycol, is an alcohol with two hydroxyl groups. It is a colourless, bittersweet liquid that dissolves in water. It is made industrially from acetaldehyde and also occurs naturally in bell peppers.

In food it is used as a solvent for flavourings and as a flavouring ingredient.

name: Castor oil
text:
Castor oil is a vegetable oil pressed from the seeds of the castor plant (Ricinus communis). About 90 percent of its fatty acids are ricinoleic acid.

As a food additive it serves as a glazing agent, an anti-caking agent, a carrier solvent and an emulsifier.

Taken by mouth in larger amounts, castor oil acts as a laxative; the effect comes from ricinoleic acid released in the small intestine.

name: Cyclotetraglucose
text:
Cyclotetraglucose is a ring-shaped carbohydrate built from four glucose units. It is made from hydrolysed food starch with the help of two enzymes. The product is a syrup, or a dried white solid, made up of several sugars in which cyclotetraglucose is the largest component; it is sold as cyclotetraglucose syrup (E1504(ii)).

It is used as a carrier, and is also classed as a stabiliser.

In 2009 the Joint FAO/WHO Expert Committee on Food Additives (JECFA) evaluated it and saw no need to set a numerical acceptable daily intake.

name: Triethyl citrate
text:
Triethyl citrate is the ethyl ester of citric acid. It is a colourless, odourless liquid.

In food it is used to stabilise foams, especially as a whipping aid for egg white, and as an emulsifier and a carrier solvent, for example for flavourings. It is also a plasticiser, used in coatings for tablets and in plastics.

name: Ethanol
text:
Ethanol (ethyl alcohol) is the alcohol found in alcoholic drinks: a volatile, flammable, colourless liquid. It is produced by yeast fermentation of sugars or from petrochemicals, by hydration of ethylene.

In food production it serves as an extraction solvent and carrier solvent and as a flavouring agent.

name: Glyceryl monoacetate
text:
Glyceryl monoacetate, or monoacetin, is an ester of glycerol with one acetic acid group. It is one of the glycerine acetates formed when glycerol is esterified with acetic acid, alongside glyceryl diacetate (E1517) and glyceryl triacetate (E1518).

JECFA classes it as a carrier solvent; in 1979 it saw no need to set a numerical acceptable daily intake, grouping it with glycerol and its other acetates.

name: Glyceryl diacetate
text:
Glyceryl diacetate, also called diacetin, is the diester of glycerol with acetic acid. It consists mainly of a mixture of the 1,2- and 1,3-diacetates of glycerol, with small amounts of the mono- and triacetates. It is a clear, colourless, somewhat oily liquid that absorbs moisture.

In food it is used as a carrier, in particular for flavourings.

name: Glyceryl triacetate
text:
Glyceryl triacetate, or triacetin, is the triester of glycerol with acetic acid. It is a colourless, somewhat oily liquid. At low concentrations it tastes mildly sweet, at higher ones bitter.

In food it is used as a humectant and as a solvent and carrier for flavourings; it is also used in chewing gum. In the body, digestive lipases split it into glycerol and acetate.

name: Benzyl alcohol
text:
Benzyl alcohol is an aromatic alcohol: a clear, colourless liquid with a faint, pleasant aromatic odour. Many plants produce it, and it is found in fruits, teas and essential oils such as jasmine and ylang-ylang; it is also made industrially.

In food it is used as a carrier in flavourings, for example for liqueurs and other aromatic alcoholic drinks, chocolate and other confectionery, and fine bakery wares.

In 2019 EFSA set an acceptable daily intake of 4 mg per kg of body weight and concluded that exposure from its use as a food additive raises no safety concern.

name: Propylene glycol
text:
Propylene glycol (propane-1,2-diol) is a clear, colourless, viscous liquid that absorbs moisture. It is almost odourless and tastes faintly sweet. Food-grade propylene glycol is mainly produced from propylene oxide.

In food it is used as a humectant and as a carrier solvent, especially for flavourings and for colours, emulsifiers and antioxidants. It is also classed as an emulsifier and glazing agent.

EFSA has set an acceptable daily intake of 25 mg per kg of body weight.

name: Polyethylene glycol
text:
Polyethylene glycols (PEG, also called macrogols) are polymers of ethylene oxide, usually named with a number that roughly matches their molecular weight. Low grades such as PEG 400 are viscous liquids; grades from about PEG 3000 to PEG 8000 are white, waxy solids.

In food it serves as an antifoaming agent, carrier, glazing agent and plasticiser. A notable use is in film coatings for food supplement tablets and capsules.

Polyethylene glycol is also the basis of a number of laxatives, sold under the name macrogol.

name: Hydroxyethyl cellulose
text: Hydroxyethyl cellulose is a gelling and thickening agent derived from cellulose. It is widely used in cosmetics, household products, paints and coatings, and in capsule formulations of medicines, where it helps poorly water-soluble drugs dissolve in the digestive tract.
